īnfīnītīvus, īnfīnītīvī m.

noun, second declension

the infinitive

The later grammarians’ modus īnfīnītīvus, the term of every modern grammar: īnfīnītīvum āctīvum, passīvum, the active and passive infinitive (Traupman 229). Quintilian’s term is verbum īnfīnītum, “the unlimited verb” (see below).

Other words

  • verbum īnfīnītum — the infinitive, “the unlimited verb”

    also used · classical · Quint. 9.3.9: cum īnfīnītō verbō sit ūsus prō appellātiōne; Quint. 1.6.8: dummodo per eandem litteram in īnfīnītō exeant; Quint. 9.3.9 (Lewis & Short)

    Quintilian’s term, often with verbum left out: the form not limited by person or number. The older name; the grammars and the classroom use the later one.

Examples

  • nostrum istud vīvere triste aspexī, cum īnfīnītō verbō sit ūsus prō appellātiōne

    “I have seen that sad living of ours”, where he has used an infinitive in place of a nounQuint. 9.3.9

  • Dīc īnfīnītīvum āctīvum hujus verbī, praesentī tempore.

    Give the present active infinitive of this verb.Traupman 229

See also mood, verb, gerund, grammar.
